title: Alcaraz Keeps Winning — Even With a Sore Leg
summary:
Carlos Alcaraz is on fire — and now he is through to the knockout stage of the ATP Finals. The 23-year-old Spaniard outclassed world number five Daniil Medvedev 6-2, 6-4 in just 72 minutes in Turin, controlling the match from start to finish.

It was Alcaraz's 11th win in a row. The seven-time major winner has been in sensational late-season form, following back-to-back titles at the Vienna Open and the Paris Masters. He even warned his rivals after his first match, a statement win over Frances Tiafoe, that he has never felt better at this stage of the season.

There was one worry. Alcaraz finished the match with heavy strapping on his upper-left leg, and later said he had felt "a little problem" with his hamstring. He was already leading by a set and a break when he received treatment. "Right now I'm just feeling OK," he said. "We will see with my team and physio, but I think the rest of today and tomorrow are really going to be important days ahead of me."

Asked what pleased him most about his performance, Alcaraz replied: "Everything". "We could see in [Medvedev's] first match that he was serving very well. I returned really well, really aggressively, and really deep," he added. "I think I just hit the ball in a sweet spot every time. I'm really happy about it."

His place in the semi-finals was confirmed by Tiafoe's win against Flavio Cobolli, and Alcaraz is scheduled to face Cobolli in his final group match on Friday. It is easy to forget that Alcaraz spent four months out with a wrist injury — he has won three titles and lost just twice in 24 matches since returning at the US Open in August.
why_it_matters: Alcaraz is one of the world's best young players, and his winning run — despite a sore leg — shows how form and fitness decide who lifts the biggest trophies.

background_read: Tennis is played in tournaments, and the ATP Finals is a season-ending event for the best men's players of the year.
Players first compete in groups, and the best go through to the knockout stage, where losing a match means going home.
A hamstring is a muscle at the back of the upper leg, and players often wear strapping — tape or bandages — to support an injured leg.
Winning many matches in a row is called a winning streak, and it shows a player is in great form.
